title: CA1 Pyramidal Cells
intro: CA1 pyramidal cells are the hippocampus's main output neurons and probably the most recorded neurons in neuroscience. Many of them are place cells, firing when an animal is in one part of its environment. Their long apical dendrite receives two separate streams, CA3 input on the proximal dendrites and entorhinal input on the distal tuft, and the coincidence of the two triggers dendritic plateaus that create new place fields in a single trial.

items: Morphology: soma in stratum pyramidale; basal dendrites in stratum oriens; an apical trunk through stratum radiatum (where Schaffer collaterals from CA3 arrive) ending in a tuft in stratum lacunosum-moleculare (where entorhinal layer 3 input arrives). About 30,000 excitatory synapses per cell in rat (Megias et al. 2001).
Firing: regular spiking with adaptation in slices; in vivo, single spikes and 'complex spikes', bursts of 2 to 6 spikes with decreasing amplitude, triggered by dendritic calcium events.

Place cells: in a given environment roughly a third to a half of CA1 cells have a place field, typically one, with in-field rates of 5 to 40 Hz and near silence elsewhere (O'Keefe & Dostrovsky 1971; Wilson & McNaughton 1993). They show phase precession: spikes occur at earlier phases of the theta rhythm as the animal crosses the field (O'Keefe & Recce 1993).

Dendrites: back-propagating action potentials attenuate along the trunk because A-type potassium channel density rises with distance (Hoffman et al. 1997); the h-current also increases with distance, normalising the timing of distal inputs (Magee 1999). Thin oblique dendrites generate local sodium and NMDA spikes (Losonczy & Magee 2006).
Plasticity: Schaffer collateral-to-CA1 synapses are where long-term potentiation was first characterised in detail, with NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP and spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

Behavioural timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP): a single dendritic plateau potential lasting hundreds of milliseconds, driven by entorhinal input to the tuft, potentiates all synapses active within a window of seconds before or after it, creating a place field in one lap (Bittner et al. 2015; Bittner et al. 2017; Milstein et al. 2021). This is a learning rule very different from STDP.

Poirazi, Brannon and Mel (2003): a detailed CA1 model with 183 compartments whose response to synaptic input was well predicted by a two-layer neural network: each thin dendritic branch applies a sigmoid to its summed input, and the soma sums the branches. This is the origin of the 'neuron as two-layer network' idea used in HTM and dendritic machine learning.

Migliore and colleagues: a series of CA1 models (Migliore et al. 1999, 2018) with distance-dependent A- and h-currents, used to study back-propagation, synaptic integration and how much variability across cells matters; Migliore et al. (2018) fitted many morphologies to a common set of features.
Golding, Kath and Spruston (2001) and Katz et al. (2009): models of how distal and proximal input interact via dendritic spikes.

Plasticity models: Clopath et al. (2010) voltage-based STDP fitted to cortical and hippocampal data; Milstein et al. (2021) a BTSP rule with eligibility and instructive signals; calcium-based rules (Shouval, Bear & Cooper 2002; Graupner & Brunel 2012) fitted to CA1 synapses.

Network and full-scale models: Bezaire et al. (2016) full-scale CA1 (point-like reduced cells, nine types); Blue Brain's full rat CA1 model (Romani et al. 2024); Hippocampome.org Izhikevich parameters for CA1 pyramidal cells (Venkadesh et al. 2018).
Abstract place-cell models: Gaussian place-field rate models; oscillatory interference models of phase precession; CA1 as a comparator of CA3 recall and entorhinal input (Lisman & Otmakhova 2001).

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: If you want neurons that combine two input streams non-linearly, the CA1 and L5 pyramidal cells are the biological templates: separate compartments for the two streams, with plateaus or calcium spikes when they coincide.
Poirazi's two-layer abstraction is cheap to implement: give each neuron several dendritic subunits with a sigmoid or threshold each, and sum them at the soma.

BTSP is worth knowing as an alternative to STDP: one-shot learning gated by a plateau, with an eligibility window of seconds. It suits a column that must learn a new object or location from a single exposure.
Place cells are a useful test: a population that learns location-specific firing from grid-like or sensory input is a quick check of your learning rules.
